messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark is a 58-year-old dentist who has been practicing in a midsize suburban town for nearly three decades. He lives with his wife, Laura, in the same house where they raised their two children, now grown and living out of state. What he cannot bring himself to talk about, even to Laura, began on a Saturday evening two years ago. Driving home from a rare late appointment, he was pulled over by a patrol officer. The official report states that the officer misidentified Mark’s vehicle as matching a suspect from an earlier incident. Within seconds of approaching the car, the officer ordered him out, forced him to the ground, and struck him repeatedly with a baton while shouting commands Mark could not process. He felt cracking pain in his ribs and a searing blow to his lower back. The encounter ended only when a supervisor arrived and recognized the mistake. No charges were filed. The officer was placed on administrative leave and later reinstated. There was no apology, no disciplinary action that Mark ever saw.

In the months that followed, Mark noticed a change he could not name. The memory of that night felt as though it belonged to someone else—something he had watched on a screen rather than lived. Yet when the memory returned, unbidden, it was anything but distant. He would hear the officer’s voice yelling, the thud of the baton, the gravel scraping his cheek. And he would feel the same sharp pain in his ribs and lower back, even though the bruises had healed long ago. He began to believe that there must be something about him that had caused the violence. He replayed the moment he reached for his license, wondering if his hand had moved too fast, if his tone had been wrong. He told himself that if he had been a different kind of man—calmer, more submissive, less noticeable—it would not have happened.

He started to avoid anything that might stir emotion, positive or negative. He stopped listening to music in the car because a song could lift his mood, and he found that unacceptable. He also began steering clear of any potentially stressful situation: he declined invitations to family gatherings, stopped attending his weekly poker game, and limited his dental practice to routine cleanings and fillings, referring complex cases to colleagues. At the office, he found himself scanning every waiting patient as a potential threat. Strangers approaching him in ordinary settings—a man asking for directions, a woman at the grocery store checkout—made his heart race and his hands tremble. He could no longer sit with his back to a door. At restaurants, he would insist on a booth facing the entrance, and at home he moved his armchair to face the hallway. His sleep became fragmented; he would lie awake for hours, replaying the officer’s shouted commands, or jolt awake in the dark, convinced someone was entering the bedroom.

These strategies eroded his life quietly. His wife began to complain that he was distant, that he had become a stranger in their own home. His practice lost a few longtime patients who sensed his unease. He stopped going to the local hardware store where the clerk always greeted him too cheerfully. The world outside his dental chair had grown treacherous, and the only way to manage it was to shrink his orbit.

What finally brought Mark to seek help was a moment of quiet desperation. He had spent a Sunday afternoon in his home office, curtains drawn, refusing to answer the phone when his sister called. He looked at the framed photograph of his children on his desk and felt nothing. His life, he thought, had been destroyed. What happened to him was deeply unjust, and nothing—absolutely nothing—had been done about it. He was not angry anymore; he was hollow. The next morning he called a therapist who specialized in trauma. He did not know if talking could change anything, but he was afraid of who he had become, and more afraid that this was all that was left.
